## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}

Derive ex = ex, derive constant is zero etc.

Derivative is again one of those words that somehow rotten us.
Most of you might remember how to calculate the derivative, study the sign of the derivative etc.
This is not about highschool test.
Yet, it is a simple concept, and like function probably use that all the time.
Derivative is essentially speed (you might remember that from physics and movement of an object).


How do you calculate speed? Distance over the time it takes to run the distance.
So for a same amount of time (say one minute), car 1 travels 1 km and car 2 travels 2 km, then car 2 is faster than car 1, or the speed of car 2 is higher than the speed of car 1.

Interpretation from visual.

Now, imagine we plot a function (see @sec-function_viz) about relationship between function and visualization.
if x is time and y is position at a given time.
Let's plot x0 and  x1 is one minute after x0. y0 and y1 position and y2 position after a minute
```{r echo = FALSE}
dat <- data.frame(
    car = as.factor(c(1, 1, 2, 2)),
    time = c(0, 1, 0, 1),
    location = c(0,1,0,2))

ggplot(dat, aes(x = time, y = location, color = car)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line()+
    theme_bw()
```
What is then speed of car 1, 1km/minute = 60 km per hour, and the speed of car 2 is 2km/minute = 120 km per hour.

Graphically, it is just yfinal - yinitial/ xfinal - xinitial.
So if we look at the angle in the rectangular triange with respect to the x axis, speed is coté opposé (y2 -y1) divided by coté adjacent x2 - x1.

the steeper the hypothenus the faster the car is

## Formal {.unnumbered}
Now, unfortunately, the mathematical rigourous definition is
lim f(x + h) - f(x)/ h when h goes to zero.

Well, the other definition which is similar is f(x2) - f(x1)/ x2 - x1 where x2 - x1 = h.

You might recognize how large is the difference between the images.

So what is the f' things that we have to learn?
Well, it is just a shortcut so we don't have to calculate the limit.
So yes, it is painful but it makes life easier.

In calculus, the derivative of a function measures its instantaneous rate of change with respect to its independent variable. Geometrically, it represents the slope of the tangent line to the function's curve at a given point.
Rigorously, the derivative is defined using the mathematical concept of a limit, which formalizes the process of letting a secant line approach a tangent line.
Here are the rigorous formal definitions of the derivative from foundational calculus and mathematical analysis textbooks.

1. The Standard Single-Variable Definition
This is the standard definition found in foundational calculus. It defines the derivative at a specific point as the limit of a difference quotient.

Textbook Source
Book: Calculus (8th Edition, 2016)
Author: James Stewart
Publisher: Cengage Learning

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 2 ("Limits and Derivatives"), Section 2.7, Stewart defines the derivative of a function f at a specific number a:
Definition: "The derivative of a function f at a number a, denoted by
​$f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$ if this limit exists."

An equivalent alternative formulation often used to emphasize the target point x approaching a is also provided:
$f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$

## If you want to know more {.unnumbered}


<!--
1. The Differentiable Function Definition
When the derivative exists at every point within an open interval, it defines a completely new function, f′(x).

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Real Analysis (4th Edition, 2011)
Authors: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert
Publisher: John Wiley & Sons

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 6 ("Differentiation"), Section 6.1, the authors formalize the derivative as a functional mapping over an interval I⊆R:
Definition: "Let I⊆R be an interval, let f:I→R, and let c∈I. We say that a number L is the derivative of f at c if given any ε>0 there exists a δ>0 such that if x∈I satisfies 0<∣x−c∣<δ, then

$\left| \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} - L \right| < \varepsilon$

In this case, we write f′(c)=L. If f has a derivative at every point of a subset D⊆I, we say that f is differentiable on D, and the function f′:D→R is called the derivative of f on D."

This ε-δ formulation strips away the informal vocabulary of "approaching" to establish a rigorous topological constraint.

1. High-Dimensional Generalization: The Total Derivative
In multivariable calculus and advanced mathematical analysis, the derivative cannot be defined simply as a quotient because dividing by a vector is mathematically undefined. Instead, the derivative is rigorously defined as a linear transformation that best approximates the function locally.

Textbook Source
Book: Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd Edition, 1976)
Author: Walter Rudin
Publisher: McGraw-Hill

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 9 ("Functions of Several Variables"), Rudin defines the total derivative for a mapping from R^n to R^m:

Definition: "Suppose E is an open set in R^n, f maps E into R^m, and x∈E. If there exists a linear transformation A of R^n into R^m such that
$\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{|f(x + h) - f(x) - Ah|}{|h|} = 0$
then f is said to be differentiable at x, and we write f′(x)=A.

The linear transformation A is called the differential or the total derivative of f at x."

(Note: In standard coordinate bases, this unique linear transformation A is represented by the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives). -->
